outline: In a plane, write a vector as $x\mathbf{i}+y\mathbf{j}$ using signed horizontal and vertical components. Add vectors component by component to find a resultant. Magnitude is $\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ and direction is fixed by a reference axis and the signs of the components. Resolve a vector of magnitude $V$ at angle $\theta$ above the positive horizontal as $(V\cos\theta)\mathbf{i}+(V\sin\theta)\mathbf{j}$. Displacement, velocity, acceleration and force all obey these vector rules. For constant velocity, divide change in displacement by time; for constant acceleration, divide change in velocity by time.

misconceptions.refutation: Perpendicular components form a right triangle, so magnitude is $\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$.

misconceptions.statement: A resultant is found by adding the magnitudes of all vectors.
misconceptions.refutation: Add corresponding signed components first; only then find the resultant magnitude.
misconceptions.contrast: Opposite vectors can cancel even though both have positive magnitudes.

misconceptions.statement: The horizontal component of a vector at an angle from the horizontal is $V\sin\theta$.
misconceptions.refutation: The horizontal component is adjacent to that angle and equals $V\cos\theta$.

misconceptions.statement: Velocity equals position divided by time even when the initial position is nonzero.
misconceptions.refutation: Velocity at constant rate is change in displacement divided by elapsed time.
misconceptions.contrast: Subtract the initial position vector before dividing.

misconceptions.statement: Acceleration is the change in speed divided by time.
misconceptions.refutation: Acceleration is change in the velocity vector divided by time.
misconceptions.contrast: A change of direction can give acceleration without changing speed.

worked.problem: Find the magnitude and direction of $3\mathbf{i}+4\mathbf{j}$, measured anticlockwise from positive $\mathbf{i}$.

steps.do: Identify horizontal component $3$ and vertical component $4$.
steps.why: Their signs place the vector in quadrant I.
Direction must name a reference axis and sense of rotation.

worked.problem: A particle moves at constant velocity from $2\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j}$ m to $8\mathbf{i}+9\mathbf{j}$ m in 3 s. Find its velocity and speed.

steps.why: Velocity uses change in displacement, including both signed coordinates.
Velocity is displacement change per unit time at constant velocity.
Speed is the magnitude of the velocity vector.

faded.problem: A particle moves at constant velocity from $\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}$ m to $13\mathbf{i}+10\mathbf{j}$ m in 4 s. Find its speed.

items.explanation: The components are perpendicular, so use Pythagoras: $|\mathbf{v}|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$.
hints: Draw the component triangle.
Use the two perpendicular component lengths.
Square both components before combining them.

items.stem: For $\mathbf{a}=[[x]]\mathbf{i}+[[y]]\mathbf{j}$ and $\mathbf{b}=[[u]]\mathbf{i}-[[v]]\mathbf{j}$, find the magnitude of $\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}$.
items.explanation: Add signed horizontal and vertical components, then take the magnitude of the resulting vector.
hints: The second vector has a negative vertical component.
Add the horizontal and vertical components separately.
Form the resultant before using Pythagoras.

items.explanation: Add like components: $3-5=-2$ and $4+2=6$. Magnitudes are not added to obtain vector components.
hints: Treat $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ separately.
Keep the negative sign of the second horizontal component.
Add each pair of signed coefficients.

items.stem: A force of magnitude $10\,\mathrm{N}$ acts $30^\circ$ above the positive horizontal. Explain how to resolve it into $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ components.
items.explanation: The horizontal side is adjacent to the angle, and the vertical side is opposite it. Both are positive in this quadrant.
hints: Sketch a right triangle with the angle at the horizontal.
Label adjacent and opposite sides.
Apply cosine to the adjacent side and sine to the opposite side.

rubric.point: The horizontal component is $10\cos30^\circ=5\sqrt3\,\mathrm{N}$.
The vertical component is $10\sin30^\circ=5\,\mathrm{N}$.

items.stem: A force is $-6\mathbf{i}+8\mathbf{j}\,\mathrm{N}$. Find its magnitude and direction, measured anticlockwise from the positive $\mathbf{i}$ direction.
items.explanation: Pythagoras gives $\sqrt{(-6)^2+8^2}=10$. The vector is in quadrant II, so the direction is $180^\circ-\tan^{-1}(8/6)\approx126.87^\circ$.
hints: Locate the quadrant from the component signs.
Use Pythagoras for magnitude.
Find the reference angle, then adjust it for quadrant II.

rubric.point: The magnitude is $10\,\mathrm{N}$.
The direction is approximately $126.87^\circ$ anticlockwise from positive $\mathbf{i}$.

items.stem: A particle moves at constant velocity from $[[x0]]\mathbf{i}+[[y0]]\mathbf{j}\,\mathrm{m}$ to $[[x1]]\mathbf{i}+[[y1]]\mathbf{j}\,\mathrm{m}$ in $[[t]]\,\mathrm{s}$. Find the magnitude of its velocity.
items.explanation: Subtract the initial position to get displacement, divide each component by time, and then find speed as the velocity magnitude.
hints: Work with a change in position.
Subtract initial coordinates from final coordinates.
Divide the displacement magnitude by elapsed time.

items.stem: A velocity changes at constant acceleration from $[[ux]]\mathbf{i}+[[uy]]\mathbf{j}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ to $[[vx]]\mathbf{i}+([[vy]])\mathbf{j}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ in $[[t]]\,\mathrm{s}$. Find the magnitude of the acceleration.
items.explanation: Acceleration is the change of the velocity vector divided by time; subtract components before calculating its magnitude.
hints: Use velocity vectors, not just speeds.
Subtract the initial velocity component by component.
Find the magnitude after dividing by time.

items.stem: Find the constant velocity when displacement changes from $2\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j}\,\mathrm{m}$ to $8\mathbf{i}+9\mathbf{j}\,\mathrm{m}$ in $3\,\mathrm{s}$.
items.explanation: The displacement change is $(8-2)\mathbf{i}+[9-(-3)]\mathbf{j}=6\mathbf{i}+12\mathbf{j}\,\mathrm{m}$; dividing by 3 s gives the velocity. Dividing final position alone by time ignores the starting position.
hints: Find the displacement change first.
Subtract the initial vector, including its negative component.
Divide each resulting component by the elapsed time.

items.stem: Explain why a particle can have non-zero acceleration while its speed remains constant.
items.explanation: Constant speed fixes the magnitude of velocity, but the velocity vector may turn; a change in velocity over time is acceleration.
hints: Distinguish speed from velocity.
Consider what happens when direction changes.
Use the definition of acceleration.

rubric.point: Velocity has direction as well as magnitude, so a change in direction changes velocity.
Acceleration is change in velocity divided by time.

items.stem: A constant force is $6\mathbf{i}-8\mathbf{j}\,\mathrm{N}$ and a second constant force is $-2\mathbf{i}+5\mathbf{j}\,\mathrm{N}$. Calculate the resultant force and its magnitude.
items.explanation: Add signed force components to get $4\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j}$ N. Its magnitude is $\sqrt{4^2+(-3)^2}=5$ N.
hints: Combine forces as vectors.
Add horizontal and vertical parts separately.
Use Pythagoras on the resultant components.

rubric.point: The resultant force is $4\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j}\,\mathrm{N}$.
Its magnitude is $5\,\mathrm{N}$.

items.stem: A displacement is $(-12\mathbf{i}+5\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m}$, where $\mathbf{i}$ points east and $\mathbf{j}$ points north. Find (a) its exact magnitude and (b) its three-figure bearing, to the nearest degree.
items.explanation: Pythagoras gives $\sqrt{(-12)^2+5^2}=13\,\mathrm{m}$. The displacement is west of north by $\tan^{-1}(12/5)\approx67.38^\circ$, so its clockwise bearing from north is $360^\circ-67.38^\circ\approx293^\circ$.
hints: Locate the compass quadrant using both component signs.
Use Pythagoras for magnitude and a right triangle for the angle from north.
Bearings are measured clockwise from north; account for the westward component.

items.stem: A force of magnitude $12\,\mathrm{N}$ acts at $30^\circ$ west of north. With $\mathbf{i}$ east and $\mathbf{j}$ north, find its signed vector components.
items.explanation: The angle is measured from north, so the northward component is $12\cos30^\circ=6\sqrt3\,\mathrm{N}$ and the westward component is $-12\sin30^\circ=-6\,\mathrm{N}$. The component pair with horizontal magnitude $6\sqrt3$ swaps the adjacent and opposite sides; the other incorrect pairs reverse a required compass sign.
hints: Sketch the force arrow and label north and east.
Identify the component adjacent to the angle measured from north.
Use sine for the opposite component, cosine for the adjacent component, then assign compass signs.

items.stem: A particle moves at constant velocity from position $(4\mathbf{i}-7\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m}$ to $(-8\mathbf{i}+9\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m}$ in $4\,\mathrm{s}$. Find (a) its complete velocity vector, (b) its speed and (c) its direction, measured anticlockwise from positive $\mathbf{i}$, to the nearest degree.
items.explanation: Subtracting positions gives $\Delta\mathbf{r}=(-12\mathbf{i}+16\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m}$, hence $\mathbf{v}=(-3\mathbf{i}+4\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and speed $5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The velocity is in quadrant II, so its direction is $180^\circ-\tan^{-1}(4/3)\approx127^\circ$ anticlockwise from positive $\mathbf{i}$.
hints: Use the change in position rather than the final position alone.
Divide each displacement component by the elapsed time; speed is the resulting vector magnitude.
Subtract initial coordinates with brackets, then use the velocity signs to choose the direction quadrant.

items.stem: A particle has constant acceleration. Its velocity changes from $(-5\mathbf{i}+7\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ to $(7\mathbf{i}-2\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ in $3\,\mathrm{s}$. Show that its acceleration is $(4\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, showing the subtraction of each component.
items.explanation: Use $\mathbf{a}=(\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u})/3$: the component changes are $7-(-5)=12$ and $-2-7=-9$. Dividing both by $3\,\mathrm{s}$ gives $\mathbf{a}=(4\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.
hints: Start from the vector definition of constant acceleration.
Subtract the entire initial velocity vector before dividing by time.
Write each change as final component minus initial component, retaining brackets around negative values.

M1-2.1.motivate: Two forces can partly cancel even when each is large. A vector diagram or signed components lets you predict the actual combined force, rather than just adding two positive magnitudes.
M1-2.1.establish:
A vector has both magnitude and direction. In a plane, $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ are perpendicular unit vectors along the positive horizontal and vertical axes. Write $\mathbf{v}=x\mathbf{i}+y\mathbf{j}$ with signs showing direction. Its magnitude is $\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$. To give its direction, name the reference axis and sense of rotation, then use the component signs to select the quadrant. The resultant of several vectors is their componentwise sum; alternatively, draw the vectors head to tail in a vector diagram. A vector of magnitude $V$ at angle $\theta$ above the positive horizontal resolves into $(V\cos\theta)\mathbf{i}+(V\sin\theta)\mathbf{j}$.
Prerequisite bridge: recall signed arithmetic, Pythagoras and right-triangle trigonometry. Fix the axes before calculating; the modelling assumptions in M1-1.1 tell you what object and forces your vector represents.
M1-2.1.connect: These same component rules apply to displacements, velocities, accelerations and forces. Once a resultant is known in components, its magnitude and direction describe the combined effect.
M1-2.1.note:
- Write signed components using $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$.
- Add like components before finding resultant magnitude.
- Use $|x\mathbf{i}+y\mathbf{j}|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ and check the quadrant for direction.
- Resolve from the horizontal with $V\cos\theta$ horizontally and $V\sin\theta$ vertically.
M1-2.1.self_explain: Why might the magnitude of the resultant of two forces be smaller than the magnitude of either force?
M1-2.1.plain_words: A vector tells you how much and in which direction. Its two signed components are instructions along perpendicular axes. Combine those instructions first, then find the length and direction of the combined arrow.

forms.name: Signed resultant
wordings: Find the resultant force in unit-vector form.
forms.example: For forces $(9\mathbf{i}-4\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{N}$ and $(-14\mathbf{i}+10\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{N}$: first group like components, then calculate $(9-14)\mathbf{i}+(-4+10)\mathbf{j}=(-5\mathbf{i}+6\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{N}$. Opposing components cancel partly; adding the two positive lengths would lose direction.

Obtain $(7\mathbf{i}-9\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{N}$ or an equivalent vector.

forms.name: Magnitude and direction
wordings: Find the magnitude and direction, anticlockwise from the positive horizontal.
forms.example: For $\mathbf{R}=(-9\mathbf{i}+12\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{N}$: (1) signs put it in quadrant II; (2) $|\mathbf{R}|=\sqrt{81+144}=15\,\mathrm{N}$; (3) the acute angle is $\tan^{-1}(12/9)=53.1^\circ$, giving direction $180^\circ-53.1^\circ=126.9^\circ$ anticlockwise from positive $\mathbf{i}$. A magnitude answer is a scalar, so remove the unit vectors.
forms.check: Find the exact magnitude and direction of $(-8\mathbf{i}-15\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{N}$, measured anticlockwise from positive $\mathbf{i}$. Give the angle to one decimal place.

rubric.point: Use Pythagoras and obtain magnitude 17 N.
Use quadrant III and obtain 241.9 degrees anticlockwise from the stated axis; accept equivalent exact angle before rounding.

forms.name: Resolve from a stated axis
wordings: Resolve a force whose angle is measured from the vertical.
forms.example: A force of $18\,\mathrm{N}$ points up and left at $40^\circ$ to the upward vertical. (1) The vertical component is adjacent to this angle, so its size is $18\cos40^\circ$. (2) The horizontal component is opposite, size $18\sin40^\circ$. (3) Apply signs: $\mathbf{F}=(-18\sin40^\circ\mathbf{i}+18\cos40^\circ\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{N}\approx(-11.6\mathbf{i}+13.8\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{N}$. Check: the squared components sum to $18^2$.
forms.check: A force of $26\,\mathrm{N}$ points down and right at $30^\circ$ to the downward vertical. Find its exact horizontal and vertical components, taking right and up as positive.
forms.source: SaveMyExams/XMA01 mechanics-1/XMA01 c1.2.pdf p.6; bundle M1-2.1; perpendicular-triangle derivation

rubric.point: The horizontal component is positive and opposite the angle: 26 sin 30 = 13 N; equivalent methods accepted.
The vertical component is negative and adjacent: -26 cos 30 = -13 sqrt(3) N; equivalent methods accepted.

misconceptions.idea: Add magnitudes to obtain the resultant magnitude.
misconceptions.temptation: Each force has a positive size, so adding sizes seems natural.
misconceptions.fix: Add signed components first; opposite equal vectors have zero resultant.

misconceptions.idea: Cosine always gives the horizontal component.
misconceptions.temptation: The familiar formula was learned with an angle from the horizontal.
misconceptions.fix: Locate the stated reference axis; cosine gives the adjacent component and sine the opposite one, then assign signs.

M1-2.2.motivate: A particle can start away from the origin, or change direction without changing speed. Vector subtraction captures both effects when you calculate motion.

discover.stem: A particle moves from $2\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j}$ m to $8\mathbf{i}+9\mathbf{j}$ m in 3 s at constant velocity. Find its velocity.
discover.explanation: Subtract the first displacement from the second, then divide each component by 3 s.

M1-2.2.establish:
Displacement, velocity, acceleration and force are vectors in a plane, so their horizontal and vertical components carry signs and combine componentwise. For constant velocity, $\mathbf{v}=(\mathbf{r}_2-\mathbf{r}_1)/\Delta t$: change in displacement divided by elapsed time. Its magnitude is speed. For constant acceleration, $\mathbf{a}=(\mathbf{v}_2-\mathbf{v}_1)/\Delta t$: change in velocity divided by elapsed time. Subtract the entire initial vector, including negative components. Because velocity has direction, speed may stay constant while velocity changes. Forces also add componentwise to give a resultant force. Use m for displacement, $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ for velocity, $\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ for acceleration and N for force.
Prerequisite bridge: use M1-2.1 to subtract signed components and find a vector magnitude. A time reading is not always the elapsed time: subtract the two readings and retain consistent units.
M1-2.2.connect: First resolve or add vectors as in the previous idea. Then divide a change vector by time when the question asks for constant velocity or constant acceleration.
M1-2.2.note:
- Constant velocity: $\mathbf{v}=(\mathbf{r}_2-\mathbf{r}_1)/\Delta t$.
- Constant acceleration: $\mathbf{a}=(\mathbf{v}_2-\mathbf{v}_1)/\Delta t$.
- Subtract vectors component by component, keeping signs.
- Speed is velocity magnitude; resultant force is the vector sum of forces.
M1-2.2.self_explain: Why does dividing the final position vector by elapsed time fail when the particle starts away from the origin?
M1-2.2.plain_words: Velocity tells you how position changes each second, including direction. Acceleration tells you how velocity changes each second. Subtract the earlier whole vector from the later one and divide by the time between them.

forms.name: Constant velocity from timed positions
wordings: Find velocity from positions at two stated times.
forms.example: At $t=2\,\mathrm{s}$ a particle is at $(-4\mathbf{i}+7\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m}$; at $t=8\,\mathrm{s}$ it is at $(14\mathbf{i}-5\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m}$. It has constant velocity. (1) $\Delta t=8-2=6\,\mathrm{s}$. (2) $\Delta\mathbf{r}=[14-(-4)]\mathbf{i}+(-5-7)\mathbf{j}=(18\mathbf{i}-12\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m}$. (3) Divide both components: $\mathbf{v}=(3\mathbf{i}-2\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Do not divide by the final clock reading.
forms.check: At $t=3\,\mathrm{s}$ a particle has position $(5\mathbf{i}-8\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m}$ and at $t=7\,\mathrm{s}$ position $(-7\mathbf{i}+12\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m}$. Find its constant velocity.
forms.source: Pearson WME01 January 2025 examiner report, Q1 pp.3–4 and Q5 p.6; https://qualifications.pearson.com/content/dam/pdf/International-Advanced-Level/Mathematics/2018/Exam-materials/wme01-01-pef-20250306.pdf Q5

rubric.point: Subtract timed positions and use elapsed time 7 - 3 = 4 s.
Give velocity (-3i + 5j) m/s; equivalent vector notation accepted.

forms.name: Position and separation at another time
wordings: Find a later position and its distance from a fixed target.
forms.example: At $t=4\,\mathrm{s}$, $\mathbf{r}=(2\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m}$ and constant $\mathbf{v}=(-\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. (1) To reach $t=7\,\mathrm{s}$ use $3\,\mathrm{s}$, giving $\mathbf{r}(7)=(2\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j})+3(-\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j})=(-\mathbf{i}+10\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m}$. (2) A fixed target has position $(5\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m}$. Subtract: particle minus target is $(-6\mathbf{i}+8\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m}$. (3) Separation is $\sqrt{36+64}=10\,\mathrm{m}$. Reversing the subtraction changes direction but not distance.
forms.check: At $t=5\,\mathrm{s}$ a particle is at $(-2\mathbf{i}+4\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m}$ with constant velocity $(4\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Find its position at $t=8\,\mathrm{s}$ and its distance then from the fixed point $(\mathbf{i}-5\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m}$.
forms.answer: $\mathbf{r}(8)=(10\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m}$. The relative vector is $(9\mathbf{i}+6\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m}$ (or its negative), so separation is $\sqrt{117}=3\sqrt{13}\,\mathrm{m}\approx10.8\,\mathrm{m}$.
forms.source: Pearson WME01 January 2025 examiner report, Q1 pp.3–4 and Q5 p.6; https://qualifications.pearson.com/content/dam/pdf/International-Advanced-Level/Mathematics/2018/Exam-materials/wme01-01-pef-20250306.pdf Q5(b)

rubric.point: Award one point only for a final position mathematically equivalent to (10, 1) m, such as 10i + j or a column vector with components 10 and 1 in that order. Reject 10i - j and swapped components. Metres may be explicit or implicit. No intermediate working is required. Keyword matches are hints only; judge the signed components of the complete final position.

Award one point only for a final nonnegative separation mathematically equivalent to 3 sqrt(13) m = sqrt(117) m, or a correctly rounded decimal to at least two significant figures (11 m at 2 s.f., 10.8 m at 3 s.f., 10.82 m at 4 s.f.). Metres may be explicit or implicit. Reject sqrt(13), 13 and 117 as distances. No relative vector or intermediate working is required. Keyword matches are hints only; judge the complete final distance, including any coefficient and square root.

forms.name: Constant acceleration from velocities
wordings: Find acceleration from two velocity vectors and their times.
forms.example: At $t=1\,\mathrm{s}$, velocity is $(-2\mathbf{i}+9\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; at $t=6\,\mathrm{s}$ it is $(13\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, under constant acceleration. (1) $\Delta t=5\,\mathrm{s}$. (2) $\Delta\mathbf{v}=[13-(-2)]\mathbf{i}+(-1-9)\mathbf{j}=(15\mathbf{i}-10\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. (3) $\mathbf{a}=(3\mathbf{i}-2\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. Divide the change vector, not the change of two speeds.
forms.check: Under constant acceleration, velocity is $(7\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ at $t=2\,\mathrm{s}$ and $(-5\mathbf{i}+15\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ at $t=8\,\mathrm{s}$. Find the acceleration vector.
forms.source: bundle M1-2.2; SaveMyExams/TQ XMA01 mechanics-1-questions-only/TQ XMA01 c2.3.pdf p.10 (constant vector acceleration context)

rubric.point: Use change of velocity divided by elapsed time 6 s.
Obtain (-2i + 3j) with acceleration units.

forms.name: Speed versus velocity
wordings: Find speed and explain whether two equal-speed velocities are equal.
forms.example: For $\mathbf{v}=(5\mathbf{i}-12\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, speed is $\sqrt{25+144}=13\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The velocity $(-5\mathbf{i}+12\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ has the same speed but opposite direction, so the velocities differ.
forms.check: Two measured velocities are $(9\mathbf{i}+12\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and $(12\mathbf{i}+9\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Find each speed. Explain whether velocity changed and whether these two measurements prove constant speed throughout the interval.
forms.answer: Each speed is $15\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Velocity changed because direction changed. The two endpoint measurements do not establish speed at intervening times.
forms.source: SaveMyExams/XMA01 mechanics-1/XMA01 c1.2.pdf p.5; bundle M1-2.2

rubric.point: Both magnitudes are 15 m/s.
Velocity changes because direction changes despite equal magnitudes.
Equal endpoint speeds do not prove constant speed between measurements.

misconceptions.idea: Subtracting a negative component keeps it negative.
misconceptions.temptation: The minus sign inside the initial vector is overlooked.
misconceptions.fix: Keep brackets: $y_2-(-y_1)=y_2+y_1$ when the earlier coefficient is $-y_1$.

misconceptions.idea: Speed is a velocity vector or change in speed is enough for acceleration.
misconceptions.temptation: Both descriptions concern how fast the object moves.
misconceptions.fix: Speed is the scalar magnitude. Acceleration uses the entire change of velocity, including direction.

M1-2.2: Position and separation at another time
